WarningPCAs / PCoAs — the lost minefield of ordination



A principal component is a weighted combination of the variables included in one particular dataset. PC1 in one study may represent body size, while PC1 in another may represent activity, condition, or a mixture of several traits. Its meaning can change with the variables included, their scaling, and the relationships among them. A PCoA axis similarly depends on the chosen distance measure and the observations included in that study.
An SMD removes the numerical units of an outcome, but it does not make outcomes with different biological meanings equivalent. The direction of a PCA or PCoA axis is also arbitrary: the same axis can be plotted with its signs reversed. Pooling study-specific axes can therefore combine different biological responses or reverse the direction of some effects.
PCA or PCoA scores should not be included in an ordinary SMD/lnRoM meta-analysis unless all studies used a genuinely shared axis with the same biological meaning. This would require compatible variables and preprocessing, a common or demonstrably equivalent scoring rule, a prespecified way to align the direction, and group means, within-group SDs, and independent sample sizes calculated in that shared coordinate system. A meta-analysis made entirely from such shared PCA axes would be unusual; it would effectively be a meta-analysis of one consistently defined composite outcome.
Centroids alone do not provide the within-group SD needed for an SMD. Do not infer an SD from an ordination ellipse unless its exact statistical definition makes that conversion possible. PERMANOVA statistics such as pseudo-\(F\), \(R^2\), and \(p\) values describe a distance-based multivariate analysis and should not be converted into an ordinary SMD.
When possible, return to the original variables and choose outcomes that answer the biological question consistently across studies. If the original outcomes or a valid shared score cannot be obtained, record the ordination result as unavailable for the SMD analysis.

title: Continuous predictors: assumptions and interpretation
text:
As you have seen so far in this guide, effect sizes are not trivial things. Together, point estimates and sampling variances are small statistical models with their own numerical assumptions, properties, and quirks. Understanding these assumptions is essential if you want to conduct a proper and robust meta-analysis, and if you want to correctly interpret these effect sizes and the outputs of meta-analytic models.
In this section, we discuss effect sizes for describing the relationship strength between two continuous variables. These are known as measures of association. While the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient (\(r\)) is the most intuitive and widely reported metric in primary studies, its mathematical properties make it problematic for direct meta-analytic pooling. Instead, we will dive into the elegant statistical world of Fisher’s Z-transformed correlation coefficient (\(Z_r\)), our variance-stabilizing alternative.

Why can’t we just pool raw correlations?
Should make clear that many studies don’t even report \(r\), they just plot scatterplots (that they might have analyzed with linear models)
When primary studies report their results, they often present Pearson’s correlation coefficient (\(r\)). It is an appealing effect size: it carries no units, so a correlation between body mass and clutch size can be compared directly against one between soil nitrogen and plant diversity (if that makes sense to be compared, which is another question). It runs from \(-1\) (a perfect negative linear association) through \(0\) (no linear association) to \(+1\) (a perfect positive linear association).
I think we should also add how \(r\) captures both relationship and variance in a single value, which can be confusing if your last stats class was ages ago…
Convenient as it is, the raw correlation coefficient has three mathematical properties that sit awkwardly with the assumptions of standard meta-analytic models. All three trace back to a single issue: \(r\) is bounded by \(-1\) and \(+1\), and statistical estimates behave badly near hard limits.

The estimate gets squeezed against the ceiling. When the true correlation in the population is near zero, repeated studies scatter symmetrically around it. When the true correlation is strong, say \(+0.8\), there is simply less room to overshoot than to undershoot, because no estimate can exceed \(+1\). The spread of plausible estimates becomes lopsided, with a long tail on the low side. The practical cost is that confidence intervals calculated the usual way assume a symmetric spread, so they end up miscalibrated and can even extend beyond \(1\), which does not make sense. Separately, and through a different route, \(r\) is a slightly shrunken estimate of the true correlation. It is pulled toward zero, whatever its sign. That shrinkage is small (for a true correlation of \(0.5\) measured on \(20\) individuals, roughly \(0.01\)), but it is the reason unbiased alternatives to \(r\) exist (Olkin and Pratt 1958).
Precision is tangled up with the result. Meta-analysis weights each study by its precision, and this only works if precision is governed by something independent of the answer, such as sample size. For correlations it is not. The sampling variance of \(r\) is

\[
v_i = \frac{(1 - r_i^2)^2}{n_i - 1}
\tag{1}\]
which contains the correlation itself. The larger the correlation a study happens to report, the smaller its variance and the heavier its weight. A study that overestimated the correlation by chance is therefore rewarded with extra influence, and the pooled estimate is dragged away from zero. Notice that this pushes in the opposite direction to the shrinkage in point 1, above. The same entanglement distorts funnel plots and inflates the false-positive rate of Egger’s test for funnel asymmetry. The scatter narrows toward large correlations for reasons that have nothing to do with genuine precision.


Small samples make matters worse. Meta-analytic models assume each study’s estimate is drawn from a bell-shaped distribution around the true value. For correlations, that approximation holds up well with large samples and modest effects, and it breaks down when the sample is small and the correlation is strong—the combination most familiar to anyone working with a dozen populations or a handful of species.

To solve these issues, Fisher proposed a variance-stabilizing, normalizing transformation (Fisher 1921, Borenstein et al. 2021).
The statistical mechanics of \(Z_r\)

1. Fisher’s \(Z\) transformation (the point estimate)
Fisher’s transformation stretches the bounded \([-1, +1]\) interval across the entire number line, pushing the ceilings out to infinity so that estimates are no longer squeezed against them. Formally, it is the inverse hyperbolic tangent (\(\text{atanh}\)):
\[
y_i = Z_{r_i} = \text{atanh}(r_i) = \frac{1}{2} \ln\left(\frac{1 + r_i}{1 - r_i}\right)
\tag{2}\]
Should the second = sign by a \(\approx\)?
Correlations near zero barely move. Correlations near the boundaries are stretched dramatically. The result is a distribution that is close to symmetric and close to normal for samples of roughly \(10\) or more.
2. The sampling variance
The real beauty of Fisher’s transformation lies in its sampling variance. After transformation, the sampling variance depends on sample size and nothing else:
\[v_i = \text{Var}(Z_{r_i}) = \frac{1}{n_i - 3} \tag{3}\]
The effect size has vanished from the variance entirely. Studies are now weighted purely by how much data they collected, which is exactly the assumption meta-analytic models were built on. Symmetry and approximate normality come along for free.






NoteThe variance formula assumes bivariate normality



Fisher’s variance is derived assuming the two variables follow a bivariate normal distribution. This means both variables are normal but covary. See here to explore this distribution.
When the underlying data are strongly non-normal (heavy tailed) abundance counts, or ratios with a few extreme values, the true sampling variance can be noticeably larger than \(1/(n_i - 3)\), and standard errors will be too optimistic (Kowalski 1972, Hawkins 1989). This is a further reason to prefer robust variance estimation (see below) when your evidence base is built on skewed ecological data.
I guess this means that you can’t do funky things, like calculate Zr for continuous responses and a discrete predictor?


3. Back-transformation to \(r\)

We conduct all statistical modeling, random-effects estimation, and moderator tests in the \(Z_r\) metric, but \(Z_r\) values are difficult to interpret conceptually. An effect size of \(Z_r = 1.1\) means very little to our brain until we convert it back to \(r = 0.8\). We therefore back-transform final pooled estimates from our meta-analytic models, and the confidence intervals, to the intuitive correlation scale using the hyperbolic tangent (\(\tanh\)):
\[r = \tanh(Z_r) = \frac{e^{2 Z_r} - 1}{e^{2 Z_r} + 1} \tag{4}\]
In R, this looks like:

tanh(1.1)

[1] 0.800499








WarningBack-transformation is not a neutral operation



Because the conversion from \(Z_r\) to \(r\) is curved rather than straight, back-transforming a pooled estimate does not return the average of the underlying correlations. It returns something closer to their median, and the gap between the two widens as between-study heterogeneity grows. In ecology and evolution, where heterogeneity is usually substantial, a back-transformed mean will typically exaggerate the magnitude of the true average correlation.
Three practical consequences:

Interval bounds back-transform safely. Because the transformation preserves rank order, converting the two ends of a confidence or prediction interval gives valid bounds on the \(r\) scale. So, convert the endpoints, never the standard error.
Heterogeneity does not back-transform at all. Report \(\tau^2\), \(I^2\), and prediction intervals on the \(Z_r\) scale, or convert the prediction interval endpoints only. There is no meaningful “\(\tau^2\) in correlation units.”
Word your conclusion carefully. “The pooled effect corresponds to a correlation of 0.42” is defensible; “the average correlation across studies was 0.42” is not, once heterogeneity is appreciable.

Some authors (notably the Hunter–Schmidt tradition; Hunter and Schmidt (2014); Field (2001)) respond to this by pooling raw correlations with sample-size weights instead. We use Fisher’s \(Z_r\) throughout this guide because it solves three problems at once, but the choice is genuinely contested and worth considering.


Code and formula pairing: implementation in R
Let’s look at how to implement these calculations in R using metafor::escalc and basic math.
Note that in many cases, the \(Z_r\) effect sizes that you calculate in a meta-analysis will involve multiple steps. Few studies report \(r\) directly. Instead many of those studies will present scatterplot visualizations, which they analyze with linear models. To calculate \(r\) (the precursor to \(Z_r\)), you’ll have to extract the points from the scatterplot (or find their raw data) and calculate \(r\) across the points.
As such, your raw dataset will be long, with a row per measurement point and an ID to specify the summarization group to calculate \(r\). The sample size (\(n\)) will be the number of rows.
Once \(r\) and \(n\) are calculated the operation is simple. We’ll here show both calculating manually and with escalc.

# Simple demonstration of Zr transformation and back-transformation in R

# Let's say we have extracted a correlation of r = 0.6 from a study of n = 50
r_val <- 0.6
n_val <- 50

# 1. Manual Fisher's Z transformation
z_manual <- 0.5 * log((1 + r_val) / (1 - r_val))
var_manual <- 1 / (n_val - 3)

# 2. Using escalc from metafor
dat_example <- data.frame(ri = r_val, ni = n_val)
dat_zr <- escalc(measure = "ZCOR", ri = ri, ni = ni, data = dat_example)

print(paste("Manual Z:", round(z_manual, 4)))

[1] "Manual Z: 0.6931"

print(paste("escalc Z (yi):", round(dat_zr$yi[1], 4)))

[1] "escalc Z (yi): 0.6931"

print(paste("escalc Z (vi):", round(dat_zr$vi[1], 4)))

[1] "escalc Z (vi): 0.0213"

# 3. Back-transformation using tanh
r_back <- tanh(z_manual)
print(paste("Back-transformed r:", round(r_back, 4)))

[1] "Back-transformed r: 0.6"








NoteFisher’s \(Z\) in metafor



The metafor package (Viechtbauer 2010) implements Fisher’s \(Z\) transformation via the measure code "ZCOR". This is the measure you want for the workflow in this chapter.
You may also encounter "UCOR", which applies the Olkin-Pratt correction (Olkin and Pratt 1958) for the small-sample shrinkage described above. Be aware that "UCOR" returns a corrected raw correlation, not a transformed one. So it fixes the shrinkage while leaving the variance-effect entanglement fully intact. It is not an upgraded version of "ZCOR", and the two should not be mixed within a single analysis. In general, we know of few cases where "UCOR" should be used instead of "ZCOR".



Click here to see a visual demonstration of the transformation stretching effect
Let’s plot how \(r\) maps to \(Z_r\). Notice how the relationship is nearly a straight line around zero but curves sharply as it approaches the boundaries of \(-1\) and \(+1\):

r_seq <- seq(-0.99, 0.99, by = 0.01)
zr_seq <- atanh(r_seq)

plot_data <- data.frame(r = r_seq, zr = zr_seq)

ggplot(plot_data
  , aes(x = r
      ,y = zr)
  ) +
  geom_line(color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(title = "Fisher's r-to-Z transformation"
    , x = "Raw correlation (r)"
    , y = "Fisher's Z (Zr)") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray")







Not all correlations are comparable
DAMN, this is useful and fuck, didn’t think of that…Thanks Ed!!
Before converting anything, check that the correlations you have extracted are estimating the same quantity. Three common mismatches will quietly corrupt an otherwise careful meta-analysis.
Partial correlations are not zero-order correlations. A study reporting the association between temperature and growth rate after controlling for body size is reporting a different parameter from a study reporting the raw association. Pooling the two together answers no clear question. If you must include partial correlations, flag them, model them as a moderator, and adjust the sample size to account for the covariates that were controlled for (the variance is closer to \(1/(n_i - k_i - 3)\), where \(k_i\) is the number of control variables; Fisher (1924); Aloe and Thompson (2013)).
Range restriction shrinks correlations (Thorndike 1949, Sackett and Yang 2000). A study sampling across a narrow elevational band will report a weaker correlation than one spanning the full gradient, even if the underlying biology is identical. Where you can, record range or standard deviation of the predictor and use it as a moderator.
Measurement error shrinks correlations too (Spearman 1904, Hunter and Schmidt 2014). Noise proxies attenuate associations toward zero. If reliability estimates are available for some studies and not others, this becomes a source of heterogeneity you cannot see.
Handling ranked correlations: Spearman’s \(\rho\) and Kendall’s \(\tau\)

When voyaging through the literature, you will inevitably encounter studies that present raw data, scatterplots, or matrices, that need to be analyzed as \(Z_r\) but are based on ranks rather than raw values. Or you will encounter studies that do not report Pearson’s \(r\). Instead, because their data were non-normal or ranked, they reported Spearman’s rank correlation (\(\rho\) or \(r_s\)) or Kendall’s tau (\(\tau\)).
Maybe we should define these?
Because these metrics are based on ranks rather than raw values, their numeric scales are slightly compressed compared to Pearson’s \(r\). To include these studies in your meta-analysis, you can apply the following transformations to approximate their Pearson equivalents:
Spearman’s \(\rho\) to Pearson’s \(r\):
\[r \approx 2 \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6} \rho\right) \tag{5}\]
Kendall’s \(\tau\) to Pearson’s \(r\):
\[r \approx \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \tau\right) \tag{6}\]
Both formulas assume the underlying data are bivariate normal (Kendall 1948, Rupinski and Dunlap 1996), which is very often the assumption the original authors doubted when they chose a rank method in the first place. Treat the conversions as approximations.
A useful refinement: once converted and Fisher-transformed, an effect size originating from Spearman’s \(\rho\) is slightly noisier than one originating from Pearson’s \(r\). Because ranks discard some metric information, converted rank correlations have slightly lower statistical efficiency than Pearson correlations, inflating the sampling variance of \(Z_r\) by about 6% under bivariate normality (Fieller et al. 1957, Myers and Sirois 2004):
\[v_i \approx \frac{1.06}{n_i - 3} \tag{7}\]
As such, these converted effect sizes will have less influence on your meta-analytic models, which, at least is a conservative type of error.






ImportantSensitivity analyses as best practice



Never treat these conversions as magic solutions. Approximations introduce uncertainty. Always flag converted effect sizes in your dataset (e.g., is_converted = TRUE) and run sensitivity analyses. Specifically, run your meta-analytic models both with and without the converted Spearman and Kendall correlations. If your overall effect size or its uncertainty shifts substantially, you must report this and be cautious in your interpretations.


The “unit of replication” obsession
A central theme of our guide is the unit of replication. When calculating and meta-analyzing measures of association, ensuring that the unit of replication aligns across studies is paramount. Mismatches in the level of replication will alter your sample size, your sampling variance, and consequently how much influence each study has on your pooled result.
Consider a study examining the correlation between soil nitrogen and plant diversity:


Study A measures the correlation across 50 individual quadrats (\(n = 50\)).

Study B measures the correlation across 5 distinct geographic sites, where each site represents the pooled average of 10 quadrats (\(n = 5\)).

Even if both studies report an identical correlation of \(r = 0.5\), Study A carries roughly 47 units of weight against Study B’s 2. A difference of more than twentyfold (!), driven entirely by a decision about what counts as a replicate. If site is the true independent unit of replication, treating Study A’s quadrats as independent replicates is pseudoreplication (Hurlbert 1984).






NoteWeights are not simply \(n - 3\)



The figures above assume a common-effects model, where a study’s weight is one over its sampling variance. In the random-effects and multilevel models you will actually fit, weight is one over the sampling variance plus the between-study variance \(\tau^2\). That extra term acts as a floor on everyone’s uncertainty and compresses the differences between studies considerably: with a moderate \(\tau^2\) of \(0.1\), the twentyfold gap above shrinks to roughly fivefold. Large studies still dominate, but far less absolutely than the raw sample sizes suggest.


Before running your models:

Identify the true, independent unit of replication for each study.
Standardize or aggregate correlations where necessary to avoid inflating sample sizes.
When in doubt, perform sensitivity analysis by adjusting sample sizes to reflect conservative biological units of replication.

Non-independence, matrices, and tagging
Correlation coefficients frequently violate the assumption of independence. Two main traps exist in continuous predictor meta-analyses:
1. Pairwise correlation matrices (the melting trap)
Primary studies often present a correlation matrix comparing multiple traits or environmental factors. Meta-analysts sometimes “melt” these matrices and include all pairwise correlations as separate effect sizes.
For example, imagine that a study reports a pairwise matrix of grooming interactions between individuals, which is thought to be a predictor of defense interactions between individuals. Melting these matrices allows you to calculate \(r\). However, the observations in that matrix are non-independent as each individual is repeated multiple times (for each interaction with other individuals).






WarningMelted matrices cause non-independence that grows quadratically



If a study measures 5 traits on a single set of individuals, it generates \(\frac{5 \times (5-1)}{2} = 10\) pairwise correlations. Those 10 correlations share the exact same subjects. Treating them as independent data points inflates your Type I error rate, because the model behaves as though you had ten times more information than you actually collected.


To handle this non-independence:

Use multilevel meta-analysis with a random effect for study or paper identity to absorb shared variance (Noble et al. 2017).
Where the same individuals contribute to several correlations, construct an explicit variance-covariance matrix with metafor::rcalc rather than relying on random effects alone.
Combine either approach with robust variance estimation (Hedges et al. 2010, Pustejovsky and Tipton 2018) (metafor::robust, or the clubSandwich package) so that your standard errors remain trustworthy even if the assumed covariance structure is imperfect.

2. Spatial and temporal flagging
Continuous predictors in ecology and evolution often vary across spatial and temporal grains. Always record and flag metadata for:


Spatial grain: e.g., local plot size, regional \(\text{km}^2\).

Temporal grain: e.g., seasonal correlation, decadal trend.

Flag groupings: flag studies sharing common study sites, common control subjects, or common experimental treatments.

Interpretation and benchmarks: what does \(r\) mean?
When interpreting your pooled effect size, you may encounter the traditional benchmarks proposed by Jacob Cohen (1988):








Effect size class
Correlation coefficient (\(r\))
Variance explained (\(r^2\))
Interpretation



Small
\(0.1\)
\(1\%\)
Subtle effect, barely visible to the naked eye.


Medium
\(0.3\)
\(9\%\)
Visible to a careful observer; typical of many social and ecological processes.


Large
\(0.5\)
\(25\%\)
Prominent relationship; easily detectable.



These labels were offered by Cohen as a fallback for researchers with no domain knowledge to draw on, and he said so explicitly. The interpretation of effect sizes is highly context-dependent:

In evolutionary ecology, natural selection operates on tiny margins. A correlation of \(r = 0.05\)—explaining a quarter of one percent of the variance—can be strongly adaptive and shape survival over generations (Kingsolver et al. 2001, Nakagawa and Santos 2012).
In biomedical research, regular aspirin consumption has an effect on heart attack risk equivalent to \(r = 0.034\). This explains about one tenth of one percent of the variance, yet translates to thousands of lives saved annually (Rosenthal 1990).

Never apply Cohen’s benchmarks blindly. Always interpret your pooled correlations in the context of the biology, the decision costs, and the practical implications of the phenomenon.
Recommended workflow for continuous predictors
Fantastic!!!
To ensure your meta-analysis is rigorous, stick to the following workflow:


Extract raw data: Record the correlation, its sample size, the type of correlation reported, whether it is zero-order or partial, and the unit of replication.

Screen for comparability: Set aside or flag partial correlations, and note any study with obvious range restriction or unreliable measurement.

Standardize conversions: Convert any Spearman’s \(\rho\) or Kendall’s \(\tau\) to Pearson’s \(r\) equivalents. Flag these.

Calculate Fisher’s \(Z_r\): Transform raw and converted correlations using metafor::escalc(measure = "ZCOR").

Address non-independence: Check for melted matrices and shared subjects. Nest non-independent effect sizes within study using multilevel random effects.

Run models: Fit multilevel random-effects models in the \(Z_r\) metric, paired with robust variance estimation.

Test sensitivity: Re-run models excluding converted metrics, small-sample outliers, or pseudoreplicated studies.

Back-transform for reporting: Convert pooled estimates and interval endpoints back to \(r\) using tanh. Keep heterogeneity statistics on the \(Z_r\) scale, and word your conclusions to reflect what the back-transformed value actually represents.

title: Effect sizes in meta-analysis
text:
Introduction
Meta-analysis has grown to be one of the powerful methods in science. By extracting data from across the literature, a meta-analyst can answer age-old questions at scales previously unimaginable. Moreover, meta-analysis can test for and correct publication bias and can thus not only control for biases in the literature base but provide a bridge between empirical questions (i.e., what is) and metascientific questions (e.g., how scientists construct knowledge).
Meta-analysis can be really hard. Meta-analytic methods continue to proliferate, with new effect sizes, models, and methods being published constantly. The literature has become a minefield of articles and tutorials of ‘best practices’ that can be bewildering for even the most experienced meta-analyst to keep up with.
We here present a living tutorial to navigating this methodological tempest, with particular emphasis on understanding effect sizes and extracting them from a variety of data formats. This tutorial is maintained by the Collaboration for Open Science and Synthesis in Ecology and Evolution at the University of Alberta, which is led by Professor Shinichi Nakagawa—one of the principle developers of new meta-analytic methods. While many of the examples in this tutorial derive from our experiences in ecology and evolution, which is rife with messy data, we believe the contents are applicable broadly.
We hope that this tutorial, by integrating tips and tricks and statistical know-how from across the decades and into the future, can increase the consistency, reliability, and reproducibility of meta-analytic research.
Should we add more of an overview of what meta-analysis is?


How to use this tutorial
We begin by discussing the dominant effect size types, their numeric assumptions, and how to interpret them. We then discuss the nuts and bolts of planning data extraction.
We then go into detail about universal challenges in extracting and calculating effect sizes and present effect-size specific pages about how to deal with the many odd and unusual data formats that you may uncover.
We conclude with a discussion of how to convert between effect size types. Finally, we also present some additional helpful material, including descriptions of effect sizes that estimate differences in variability and magnitude between groups and effect sizes for single group descriptive statistics. These effect size types are also summarized in a cheatsheet for the many options available in metafor’s escalc function (Viechtbauer 2010)—the workhorse of effect size calculation and meta-analysis.
This tutorial is based on an R workflow and assumes that the users have a basic understanding of R. This tutorial is viewable as a webpage or you can clone the repo and run the .qmd files interactively.


Voyaging among the ghosts of data past
Meta-analyses are powerful. But they are full of tedium. And dealing with the challenges that we describe in this tutorial (hopefully in plain english) can be overwhelming.
Yet there is something beautiful and very human about doing a meta-analysis. You encounter the heartwork and hardwork of dozens or hundreds or thousands of fellow human beings. Stories from last year or 50 years ago, from people exploring, observing, experimenting, and trying to understand our universe.
These voyagers left us breadcrumbs. Sometimes as simple as a mean and a standard deviation. Sometimes as complex as some strange contour plot drawn on a piece of graph paper and scanned in 1975. Extracting their data summaries (or finding their raw datasets) brings their work to life and allows us to continue their quests.
While you struggle to deal with all the strange and bizarre and difficult and annoying decisions these voyagers sometimes made to communicate their tales, remember to feel compassion and awe for the work that came before us–these efforts to describe the mysteries of our world.


A living tutorial
This tutorial is a living document. As such, please help us keep it alive and useful. If we missed anything, if we made an error, or overlooked an extraction challenge, please file an Issue on our github page here.







References

Viechtbauer, W. 2010. Conducting meta-analyses in R with the metafor package. Journal of Statistical Software 36:1–48.

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Sometimes the world is just black and white. Individuals live or die. Organisms are present or absent. Vegetation plots burn or don’t burn.
Calculating dichotomous effect sizes requires organizing frequency data into a standard 2×2 contingency table. In ecology, this often compares an exposed or managed group to a control group across a binary outcome (e.g., mortality vs. survival, or presence vs. absence):









Target Event (e.g., Mortality)
Non-Event (e.g., Survival)
Total



Exposed (e.g., Pollutant / Stressor)
a
b
a + b


Control (e.g., Ambient Conditions)
c
d
c + d



Let’s create a running example that we’ll use throughout:

# Define dataset representing a 2x2 table for amphibian chytrid infection across two wetlands
dat_dichotomous <- data.frame(
  site = c("Wetland A", "Wetland B"),
  ai = c(15, 20), # Infected in exposed (warmed mesocosm)
  bi = c(85, 30), # Uninfected in exposed (warmed mesocosm)
  ci = c(10, 15), # Infected in control (ambient)
  di = c(90, 35)  # Uninfected in control (ambient)
)

log Odds Ratio (OR)
The Odds Ratio (OR) compares the odds of an ecological event happening in a treatment or exposed group to the odds of it happening in a control group. Odds measure the probability of an event happening versus not happening (ranging from 0 to infinity).
\[\begin{aligned}
&OR=\frac{a \times d}{b \times c} \\
\end{aligned} \tag{1}\]
Analyzing OR directly in a meta-analysis is not recommended because the values are bounded by 0 and do not approximate normality. For that reason, we log transform it so that it centers on 0 and varies from \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\).
\[\begin{aligned}
&lnOR = log(OR)\\
\end{aligned} \tag{2}\]






NoteClick to see how log transformation alters the distribution of the odds ratio






# Blah blah blah




Let’s calculate lnOR for our running example data:

# Calculate Log Odds Ratio (ln OR)
dat_or <- escalc(measure = "OR", 
                 ai = ai, bi = bi, 
                 ci = ci, di = di, 
                 data = dat_dichotomous)
dat_or


       site ai bi ci di     yi     vi 
1 Wetland A 15 85 10 90 0.4626 0.1895 
2 Wetland B 20 30 15 35 0.4418 0.1786 


To interpret odds ratios in plain english, you can exponentiate the effect sizes or model estimates (\(e^{lnOR}\)) to convert them back to Odds Ratios. Interpret Odds Ratios as follows:

OR = 1: Equal odds between the comparison groups (e.g., a stressor has no effect on mortality odds).
OR > 1: Higher odds of the event in the exposed group.
OR < 1: Lower odds of the event in the exposed group.

Let’s convert and interpret a lnOR effect of 0.18 in plain english. First, we convert it to back to an Odds Ratio:

exp(0.18)

[1] 1.197217


An odds ratio of 1.19 means 1.19 higher odds of the outcome in the exposed (treatment) wetland. There are several ways to write this in plain english:
Can someone double check this? 1. Subtract the odds ratio from 1 and multiply by 100 to calculate percentage decrease or increase: \(100 * (1 - OR)\).

The odds of the outcome occurring were 19% higher in the exposed group than the control group


Directly state the odds on a percentage scale: (\(OR * 100\))


The odds of the outcome occurring to the exposed group were 119% higher than they were for the control group


You can also take the inverse of the odds to describe the outcome for the control group: \(1/OR\)



The control group had 0.8 times higher odds of experiencing the outcome

lnOR Sampling Variance
Variance for the OR is calculated on a natural logarithmic scale:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&Var(\ln OR)=\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}+\frac{1}{d}\\
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}\]
Continuity corrections
As you can see in ?@eq-lnOR and Equation 3, if site or cohort (i.e., \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), or \(d\)) has a value of 0 (e.g., no individuals died in the control group), the effect size becomes incalculable. To resolve this, researchers apply a standard 0.5 continuity correction to all cells if a 0 is present in any cell for that particular effect size. This is done automatically by escalc:

escalc(measure = "OR",
       ai = 10, bi = 10,
       ci = 0, di = 5)


      yi     vi 
1 2.3979 2.3723 


log Risk Ratio (lnRR)
The Risk Ratio (RR), or Relative Risk, compares the absolute probability (risk) of an event in the exposed group to the risk in the unexposed group. Each risk is defined as the number of individuals experiencing the outcome divided by the total number of individuals. \[
\begin{aligned}
&n_1 = a + b\\
&n_2 = c + d\\
&RR=\frac{a/n_1}{c/n_2} \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}\]
While interpreted similarly to the OR, the RR evaluates absolute probability. For common events in a population, the RR is mathematically capped; it cannot exceed \(1/CGR\) (Comparator Group Risk). ^ Unclear. Kyle?
As with OR, for meta-analysis RR is log transformed to approximate normality and to be centered on 0. \[
lnRR = log(RR) \\
\tag{5}\]
Let’s calculate lnRR for our dataset:

# Calculate Log Risk Ratio (ln RR) utilizing the established dataset
dat_rr <- escalc(measure = "RR", ai = ai, bi = bi, ci = ci, di = di, data = dat_dichotomous)
dat_rr


       site ai bi ci di     yi     vi 
1 Wetland A 15 85 10 90 0.4055 0.1467 
2 Wetland B 20 30 15 35 0.2877 0.0767 


To interpret these effect sizes (and the final model estimates), you first convert lnRR to RR by exponentiating (\(e^lnRR\)):

exp(0.405)

[1] 1.499303


Thus an lnRR of \(0.405\) is equivalent to an RR of \(1.499\).
Interpret RR as follows:

RR = 1: Equal risk (or probability) between the comparison groups (e.g., a stressor has no effect on overall mortality risk).
RR > 1: Higher risk (or probability) of the event in the exposed group.
RR < 1: Lower risk (or probability) of the event in the exposed group.

In plain english, you can write an RR of ~1.50 as:

As with lnOR, you can subtract RR from 1 and multiply by 100 (\(100 * (1 - RR)\)). This is called the Relative Risk Reduction.


The outcome is 50% more likely in the exposure group than the control group.


You can also report RR directly, which is easiest to interpret than OR.


The exposure group was 1.50 times as likely to experience the outcome than the control group

lnRR Sampling Variance
Like lnOR, lnRR variance is calculated on the log scale:
\[Var(\ln RR)=\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{a+b}+\frac{1}{c}-\frac{1}{c+d}\]
Continuity correction
lnRR breaks down when \(a\) or \(c\) equal 0 and thus also requires a continuity correction. For lnRR, you add 0.5 to the affected group (not both groups) and add 1 to n1 or n2, respectively.






ImportantDefining the Target Event



You must rigorously define your target “event”. It can be easy to accidentally swap success with failure or fledged with failed. Switching the target (analyzing non-events instead of events) changes your metrics differently:


OR: The new estimate becomes the exact reciprocal (\(1/x\)).
RR: The estimate, its precision, and statistical significance all change dramatically—which is a troubling mathematical property of RR.

Best practice: Define the less common event as the target event to minimize mathematical errors and inter-study heterogeneity. Be sure to change your column names to be informative and to reduce data input errors. We recommend color-coding your columns in Excel to further reduce potential confusion.


When to use lnOR or lnRR
Some consider RR to be easier to interpret than OR. However, unlike lnOR, lnRR is a bounded effect size, leading to mathematical properties that make it less preferred to lnOR.
Blah blah blah.

This finding was consistently observed across three different meta-analytical scenarios, and was also observed by Sweeting and colleagues (Sweeting et al 2004).
This finding was noted despite the method producing only an approximation to the odds ratio. For very large effects (e.g. risk ratio=0.2) when the approximation is known to be poor, treatment effects were under-estimated, but the Peto method still had the best performance of all the methods considered for event risks of 1 in 1000, and the bias was never more than 6% of the comparator group risk.
In other circumstances (i.e. event risks above 1%, very large effects at event risks around 1%, and meta-analyses where many studies were substantially imbalanced) the best performing methods were the Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio without zero-cell corrections, logistic regression and an exact method. None of these methods is available in RevMan.
Methods that should be avoided with rare events are the inverse-variance methods (including the random-effects DerSimonian and Laird method) (Efthimiou 2018). These directly incorporate the study’s variance in the estimation of its contribution to the meta-analysis, but these are usually based on a large-sample variance approximation, which was not intended for use with rare events. We would suggest that incorporation of heterogeneity into an estimate of a treatment effect should be a secondary consideration when attempting to produce estimates of effects from sparse data – the primary concern is to discern whether there is any signal of an effect in the data.”

Applied Ecological Examples: Matching the Effect Size to What Your Design Provides
The effect size you can report is determined first by what your design allows you to estimate (the OR when only odds are available), and second by how the result will be used (RR for comparing effects across studies; RD for judging impact in a specific system).
Example 1
You cannot calculate the proportion of each group that experienced the event → OR only
Example: Testing whether large horns deter bird predation in beetles. Researchers collect the remains of the killed beetles (cases) and sample living beetles from the same area (controls), then compare how often the large-horn phenotype occurs in each group.
Why is OR needed?
As sampling is by outcome, the proportion of killed beetles in the dataset is set by the researcher, not by the true predation rate. With no denominator for the population at risk, RR and RD cannot be estimated. The OR can be estimated because it is the same whether sampling is by outcome or by exposure.
I’m not following this Kyle
Example 2
You can calculate the proportion of each group that experienced the event, and want to say how many times higher or lower it is → RR
Example: A two-year field experiment tracking 1,000 oak seedlings inside deer exclosures and 1,000 in adjacent open plots, with mortality as the target event.
Why is RR preferred?
All seedlings are counted at planting, so mortality risk is observed directly in each treatment. The RR gives the proportional change in mortality (e.g., “exclosures reduce mortality risk by 60%”) and is comparable across studies. Because mortality is common in open plots (~35%), the OR would be much smaller than the RR and, if reported as a relative risk, would overstate the effect of exclosures.
Example 3
You can calculate the proportion of each group that experienced the event, and want to say how many more or fewer event occurred → RD alongside RR
Example: Comparing colonisation by a specialist butterfly between isolated habitat fragments and fragments linked by a corridor: 20% of isolated patches and 35% of connected patches are colonised over the study period.
Why is RD needed (alongside RR)?
The RR (1.75) shows that corridors increase the probability of colonisation by 75% relative to isolated patches. The RD (0.15) expresses the same results as an absolute change: 15 additional patches colonised per 100, or roughly serve corridors required for each additional colonisation (NNM ≈ 6.7). Because an RR of 1.75 would correspond to a much smaller absolute gain at a lower baseline (e.g., 3 additional patches per 100 if only 4% of isolated patches were colonised), the RD is the measure needed to judge whether corridor construction justifies its cost.
Comparing odds ratio, risk ratio and risk difference
Shouldn’t one be used with rare outcomes and the other with more common outcomes?









Effect size
What it compares
Scale
Main strength
Main limitation



OR
Odds between groups
Relative

Less intuitive and can exaggerate relative effects for common events


RR

Requires known risks and depends on baseline risk


RD

Less comparable across populations with very different baseline risks



The relationship between these measures can be summarised simply:


OR vs. RR: Both describe relative effects, but OR is based on odds and RR is based on probability. They are approximately equivalent only when the outcome is rare.

RR vs. RD: Both use probability, but RR describes proportional change while RD describes the actual change in probability.

OR vs. RD: OR describes relative change on an odds scale, whereas RD describes absolute change. The same OR can produce very different RDs depending on baseline risk.

The Risk Difference (RD), or absolute risk reduction, measures the exact difference in observed risk between the experimental and control groups. This metric is ideal for weighing conservation trade-offs between a management intervention’s ecological benefits and its implementation costs.
\[
\begin{aligned}
n_1 = a + b
n_2 = c + d
&RD=\frac{a}{n_1}-\frac{c}{n_2}
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}\]
Interpret the statistical output as follows:

RD = 0: Equal risk between the comparison groups (the exposure or intervention has no absolute effect on risk).
RD > 0: Higher absolute risk of the event in the exposed group.
RD < 0: Lower absolute risk of the event in the exposed group (representing absolute risk reduction).

RD Sampling Variance
Unlike the OR and RR, the Risk Difference is measured on an absolute scale, so its variance is calculated directly on the raw scale rather than a logarithmic scale:
\[Var(RD)=\frac{a \times b}{(a+b)^3}+\frac{c \times d}{(c+d)^3}\]

# Calculate Log Risk Difference (lnRD) utilizing the established dataset

                 ai = ai, bi = bi, 
                 ci = ci, di = di,

title: Discrete outcomes between two groups
text:
The log odds ratio (lnOR) and risk ratio (lnRR) effect sizes are based on two-group contingency tables. These study designs use a discrete treatment and have a discrete binary outcome. Are they dead or alive, did they breed or not, etc. Such data looks like this, where a, b, c, d are integer count values.
These outcomes are binomial, i.e., are discrete processes with binary outcomes that occur to individuals. Individuals can be both individual organisms as well as individual sites/islands/plots, i.e., in terms of presence or absence of some binary condition.
Tertiary outcomes binomial outcomes are also possible and need to be handled with alternative effect sizes. For example, the frequency of alleles (AA, Aa, aa) in a population can be described with the Hardy-Weinburg Equilibrium effect size (Wellek et al. 2010). These are not discussed in this tutorial.

text:
log Risk Ratio (lnRR)
The risk ratio (or relative risk, lnRR) is similar to lnOR. While lnOR describes the odds of an event occurring, lnRR measures the probability of an event happening in one group relative to the others. The log risk ratio may be more easy to interpret but has numeric properties that make lnOR statistically preferable in many cases (Borenstein et al. 2021).
lnRR is defined as:
\[\begin{aligned}
&p1 = a/n1 \\
&p2 = c/n2 \\
&lnRR = log(p1/p2) \\
\end{aligned} \tag{3}\]
Assumptions

Interpretation

out <- escalc(measure = "RR",
       ai = 35, bi = 12,
       ci = 15, di = 21)

exp(out$yi[1])

A risk ratio of 1.79 indicates that the probability of survival in the drug group is 1.79 times the probability of survival in the placebo group. This follows the table and code above, where the event in the first column is survival.

text:
Continuity corrections
lnOR breaks down whenever \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), or \(d\) equal 0. To overcome this, we apply a continuity correction (Yates 1934) by adding 0.5 to all cells if any cell equals 0.
lnRR breaks down when \(a\) or \(c\) equal 0 and thus also requires a continuity correction. For lnRR, you add 0.5 to the affected group (not both groups) and add 1 to n1 or n2, respectively.
These continuity corrections are applied by escalc by default.

title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
Many effect sizes can be inter-converted (Borenstein et al. 2021, Lajeunesse 2026) These conversions make assumptions and can bias the resulting effect types (see (Poom and Wåhlberg 2022)) and should be carefully used—with sensitivity analyses to ensure that the conversions aren’t unduly influencing results.
At the same time, especially for questions with limited data, we believe that conversions are an important tool in the meta-analyst toolkit.


Effect size types


Converting effect sizes requires several assumptions. We summarize these in the table below:






Conversion
Assumption



lnOR ↔︎ SMD
Response variable is a discretized version of an underlying continuous variable


SMD ↔︎ Zr
Predictor variable is a discretized version of an underlying continuous variable


lnOR ↔︎ Zr
Response and predictor have an underlying continuous reality


SMD ↔︎ lnRoM
Homogeneity of variances between groups









Warning



What about comparing truly discrete to continuous? Are there any cases where this is desired or needed? Perhaps in behavioral data?
Because \(r_{pb}\) (point biserial correlation) is for naturally discrete groups and this can be calculated from means±sd and then you can convert to Zr (though Jacobs and Viechtbauer (2017) say you shouldn’t? because sampling variance isn’t correct? though it’s probably ok to do).
READ Jacobs and Viechtbauer (2017)



In addition to these assumptions, be careful that the data is truly comparable, especially in terms of their units of replication—otherwise the converted effect size will have vastly higher or lower weights in the final meta-analytic model.
For example, imagine you’re analyzing the effect of an introduced predator on prey abundance. Some studies present abundance correlations of the predator and prey (Zr), where the unit of replication is the number of surveys. Other studies report the presence and absence of prey species on islands with and without the predator (lnOR), for which the unit of replication is number of islands (each of which was presumably surveyed many times).
Both of these study types are relevant to the same question–—the effect of the predator on prey abundance. Likewise, converting betwee these effect sizes does not violate the assumptions in the table above because presence-absence is a discretized version of abundance. It is thus possible to convert these effect sizes via SMD to include both papers in the same model.
However, the units of replication of these study types are vastly different (study 1 = survey; study 2 = island). This means the Zr abundance correlations will have more weight than the full-island lnOR responses.
However, in many other cases, conversions will allow similar data to be compared without comparing different units of replication.
Given the assumptions and potential biases involved in converting effect sizes, we recommend that you convert minority effect sizes to the dominant effect size in your dataset after confirming that assumptions are met and that the unit of replication for all the effect sizes are equivalent. We then recommend running your models with and without these converted effect sizes, to evaluate whether the inclusion of minority effect sizes alter your results.






ImportantAlternative to conversion: reconstruct the underlying data



In some cases, converting between effect sizes can be prevented by reconstructing the underlying data of the author-presented summaries and summarizing these data into the desired analysis effect size, which can align the units of replication between studies.
See examples for SMD-type effect sizes, lnOR effect sizes, Zr effect sizes, and for non-Gaussian responses



We have digitized the primary conversion formulas and they are available in our convert_effect_sizes() function. Running the function on its own will return a table with the statistics required for each conversion.

convert_effect_sizes()


Effect type name must be specified with 'effect_type' argument
    and provide necessary variables (as named arguments, e.g., n1 = group1_n or a numeric vector).
 
Returning effect size names & required variables for reference.


   from_effect to_effect  vars_required
        <char>    <char>         <char>
1:        lnOR       SMD yi, vi, n1, n2
2:          Zr       SMD      yi, vi, n
3:           r       SMD           r, n
4:         SMD        Zr yi, vi, n1, n2
5:         SMD      lnOR yi, vi, n1, n2
6:       lnRoM       SMD yi, vi, n1, n2
7:          Zr      lnOR      yi, vi, n
8:        lnOR        Zr     yi, n1, n2


To convert an effect size, specify the from effect type and the to effect type, as well as the required statistics. Note that this function also supports full, two-step conversions from Zr to lnOR and vice versa.
We’ll now show the math and demonstrate the conversions in R. SMD is the universal solvent of these conversions and it is important to remember that SMD has multiple estimators. The most commonly used is Hedges’ \(g\), which has a small sample size bias correction factor \(J\). However, all conversion formulas convert to and from \(d\), an alternative estimator of SMD that lacks this correction factor. For that reason, the math below will skip this conversion and be written for \(d\) instead of \(g\) based on this conversion.
\[
\begin{aligned}
&J = 1-\frac{3}{4*(n_1 + n_2 - 2) - 1}\\
&d = \frac{m1-m2}{sd_{pooled}}\\
&d = \frac{g}{J}
\end{aligned}
\] Note that the default sampling variance estimator for Hedges’ g is the same estimator used for Cohen’s d (in the R package escalc. Thus no conversion from Var(d) to Var(g) is necessary.






ImportantAlternative estimators and effect size conversion



As described earlier in this tutorial, there are multiple flavors of estimators for many effect sizes including paired estimators and, for SMD, an estimator that tolerates heteroscedastic data (“SMDH”). To the best of our knowledge, there are no conversion formulas for these alterative estimators.
This means that if you are converting Zr effect sizes to add to a meta-analysis that is otherwise composed of SMD-type effect sizes, you won’t be able to use SMDH for the larger dataset. Conversely, if you have paired SMD-type data that you wish to convert to add to a meta-analysis of Zr effect sizes, you’ll have to ignore the paired design.

title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
In addition to these assumptions, be careful that the data is truly comparable, especially in terms of their units of replication—otherwise the converted effect size will have vastly higher or lower weights in the final meta-analytic model.
For example, imagine you’re analyzing the effect of an introduced predator on prey abundance. Some studies present abundance correlations of the predator and prey (Zr), where the unit of replication is the number of surveys. Other studies report the presence and absence of prey species on islands with and without the predator (lnOR), for which the unit of replication is number of islands (each of which was presumably surveyed many times).
Both of these study types are relevant to the same question–—the effect of the predator on prey abundance. Likewise, converting betwee these effect sizes does not violate the assumptions in the table above because presence-absence is a discretized version of abundance. It is thus possible to convert these effect sizes via SMD to include both papers in the same model.
However, the units of replication of these study types are vastly different (study 1 = survey; study 2 = island). This means the Zr abundance correlations will have more weight than the full-island lnOR responses.
However, in many other cases, conversions will allow similar data to be compared without comparing different units of replication.
Given the assumptions and potential biases involved in converting effect sizes, we recommend that you convert minority effect sizes to the dominant effect size in your dataset after confirming that assumptions are met and that the unit of replication for all the effect sizes are equivalent. We then recommend running your models with and without these converted effect sizes, to evaluate whether the inclusion of minority effect sizes alter your results.






ImportantAlternative to conversion: reconstruct the underlying data



In some cases, converting between effect sizes can be prevented by reconstructing the underlying data of the author-presented summaries and summarizing these data into the desired analysis effect size, which can align the units of replication between studies.
See examples for SMD-type effect sizes, lnOR effect sizes, Zr effect sizes, and for non-Gaussian responses

title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
We have digitized the primary conversion formulas and they are available in our convert_effect_sizes() function. Running the function on its own will return a table with the statistics required for each conversion.

convert_effect_sizes()

    and provide necessary variables (as named arguments, e.g., n1 = group1_n or a numeric vector).
 
Returning effect size names & required variables for reference.

1:        lnOR       SMD yi, vi, n1, n2
2:          Zr       SMD      yi, vi, n
3:           r       SMD           r, n
4:         SMD        Zr yi, vi, n1, n2

To convert an effect size, specify the from effect type and the to effect type, as well as the required statistics. Note that this function also supports full, two-step conversions from Zr to lnOR and vice versa.
We’ll now show the math and demonstrate the conversions in R. SMD is the universal solvent of these conversions and it is important to remember that SMD has multiple estimators. The most commonly used is Hedges’ \(g\), which has a small sample size bias correction factor \(J\). However, all conversion formulas convert to and from \(d\), an alternative estimator of SMD that lacks this correction factor. For that reason, the math below will skip this conversion and be written for \(d\) instead of \(g\) based on this conversion.
\[
\begin{aligned}
&J = 1-\frac{3}{4*(n_1 + n_2 - 2) - 1}\\
&d = \frac{m1-m2}{sd_{pooled}}\\
&d = \frac{g}{J}
\end{aligned}
\] Note that the default sampling variance estimator for Hedges’ g is the same estimator used for Cohen’s d (in the R package escalc. Thus no conversion from Var(d) to Var(g) is necessary.






ImportantAlternative estimators and effect size conversion



As described earlier in this tutorial, there are multiple flavors of estimators for many effect sizes including paired estimators and, for SMD, an estimator that tolerates heteroscedastic data (“SMDH”). To the best of our knowledge, there are no conversion formulas for these alterative estimators.
This means that if you are converting Zr effect sizes to add to a meta-analysis that is otherwise composed of SMD-type effect sizes, you won’t be able to use SMDH for the larger dataset. Conversely, if you have paired SMD-type data that you wish to convert to add to a meta-analysis of Zr effect sizes, you’ll have to ignore the paired design.

title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
SMD → lnOR
This conversion assumes that the response variable is continuous (e.g., undergirding the binary response of the lnOR effect type) and that it has a logistic distribution (similar to a normal distribution).
If the lnOR data was presence/absence of a species and the SMD data was abundance, we believe this assumption is satisfied, given that presence/absence are the extreme ends of abundance.
Let \(yi_{lnOR}\) and \(yi_{d}\) be the point estimate for the lnOR and Cohen’s d effect sizes and \(vi_{lnOR}\) and \(vi_{d}\) be their sampling variances:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&yi_{lnOR} = yi_d * \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}} \\
&vi_{lnOR} = vi_{d} * \frac{\pi^2}{3} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In R:

convert_effect_sizes(from = "SMD",
                     to = "lnOR",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n1 = 15,
                     n2 = 15)

This conversion assumes that the continuous data has a logistic distribution. 
Please use conversions carefully and conduct sensitivity analyses. 
Note that the 'vi' is assumed to have been calculated with `metafor::escalc` package defaults (variance of 'd' not 'g')

title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
lnOR → SMD
To convert from lnOR to Cohen’s \(d\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&yi_d = yi_{lnOR} * \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\pi} \\
&vi_d = vi_{lnOR} * \frac{3}{\pi^2} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In R:

convert_effect_sizes(from = "lnOR",
                     to = "SMD",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n1 = 15,
                     n2 = 15)

This conversion assumes that the response variable is a discretized version of a continuous variable 
with a logistic distribution for each group (which approximates the normal distribution).
Please use conversions carefully and conduct sensitivity analyses with and without converted data.

title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
SMD → Zr
This conversion assumes that a continuous variable was discretized to form the treatment and control groups of an SMD effect size. This may be the case in some situations (e.g., if treatment and control were based on the presence or absence of an independent variable treatment while the correlation was across a continuous gradient of the same variable).
To convert from SMD to Zr, we first convert \(d\) to the correlation coefficient \(r\) and then to Zr, using a correction factor \(a\) for cases where \(n_1 \neq n_2\). Let \(yi_{Zr}\) and \(yi_d\) be the point estimate for Zr and Cohen’s d:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&a = \frac{(n_1 + n_2)^2}{n_1*n_2} \\
&r = \frac{yi_d}{\sqrt{yi_d^2 + a}} \\
&r \leftarrow \min(1, \max(-1, r_i))\\
&yi_{Zr} = atanh(r)\\
\end{aligned}
\]
And the sampling variance of Zr (\(vi_{Zr}\)): \[
\begin{aligned}
&n = n1 + n2 \\
&vi_{Zr} = \frac{1}{(n - 3)} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In R:

convert_effect_sizes(from = "SMD",
                     to = "Zr",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n1 = 15,
                     n2 = 15)

This conversion assumes a continuous variable was dichotomized to create the treatment and control groups. 
Note that the 'vi' is assumed to have been calculated with 'metafor::escalc' defaults (variance of 'd' not 'g'). 
Like usual, be careful :) 


    yi_trans   vi_trans
       <num>      <num>
1: 0.4474395 0.03703704

This can be done in escalc directly with the measure “ZBIS”, which calculates teh biserial correlation coefficient and converts it to Zr.

However, Jacobs and Viechtbauer (2017) advised against comparing this to correlation coefficients calculated from 2 continuous variables (\(r\)) or from one artificially discretized variable (\(r_b\)).

title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
Zr → SMD
First, convert the point estimate of Zr (\(yi_{Zr}\)) to the correlation coefficient \(r\) and calculate the variance of \(r\) (\(vi_r\)): \[
\begin{aligned}
&r = tanh(yi_{Zr}) \\
&vi_r = \frac{(1-r^2)^2}{(n-1)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Then calculate the point estimate (\(yi_d\)) and variance (\(vi_d\)) of Cohen’s d:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&yi_d = \frac{2*r}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} \\
&vi_d = \frac{4*vi_r}{(1-r^2)^3} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In R:

convert_effect_sizes(from = "Zr",
                     to = "SMD",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n = 50)

'yi' is assumed to be 'Zr' (r-to-z transformed correlation coefficient). 
It may be preferable to supply 'r' and 'n' instead. To do so specify 'r' in the 'from' argument and provide a vector of correlation coefficients named 'r'. 
This conversion assumes that the underlying data was continuous with a bivariate normal distribution, with the two groups created by dichotomozing one of the two variables. 
Please use conversions carefully and conduct sensitivity analyses
